I should like to make a suggestion with regard to the business today, Mr. Speaker. As the House will recall, I called as business for today government order 67 and government order 76. From inquiries I have made, I gather there is some prospect that if the debates took their usual course they might well be disposed of by one o'clock today.
Hon. members will have noted that there is a motion on the Order Paper in the name of the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, and I suggest the House might make an order along the following lines: that the House proceed with other routine proceedings and the question period now, that the two government orders announced for today be considered and dealt with by one o'clock today, and that the House should then move to consider the motion in the name of the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador.
On this basis the business called for today could be dealt with, the House could have a question period and the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador along with 21774-5
his hon. friends from Newfoundland, including the Minister of Transport, would have an opportunity to deal with the question of Labrador transportation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the President of the Privy Council makes a suggestion we always stand back and examine it with great care. We are prepared to be very accommodating. On the instructions of my leader I suggest we proceed with the question period in the normal way and that the order in the name of my hon. friend should then be called.
I agree with the Leader of the House to this extent, that the two items of business called for today could probably be dealt with, and receive the proper examination, within an hour. But it is our view, and the view of the mover of the motion, that his motion should at least be the subject of a reasonable amount of discussion in the House. We therefore make the following proposal: that after the question period we should proceed with the motion, and that at three o'clock the debate would be concluded and a vote taken. We do not suggest the government has to accept this motion, but having regard to the great statements which were made yesterday about the right of this House to express its views, we feel we should have the right to express an opinion on the motion. It seems to me this is a very reasonable request to make, and I am sure that having heard it the President of the Privy Council will be bound to accept it.

The recommendation which arouses most interest among the people of Labrador is, I believe, the one which has to do with roads and highway construction. The committee recommended that the federal government consider the advisability of entering into an agreement with the Province of Quebec and Newfoundland with a view to constructing a road to connect the north of Baie Comeau with the cities of Sept lies, Manicouagan, Gagnon, Wabush, Churchill Falls and Goose Bay, of course, by using existing roads as far as possible. I am always happy when I can commend the Committee on Transport and Communications, of which I was a member back in days before many hon. gentlemen were in this House. I have good reason to know the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador is correct when he says this is one of the most hard-working committees of the House and one of the most thorough. It usually comes up with some of the best recommendations.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
Among those are the recommendations contained in this report. I say this, perhaps, with more authority than I can express judgment on some of the other matters dealt with in the committee's recommendations, because I have a personal knowledge of at least most of the matters which are discussed in this report. It is clear from the recommendations that are made that they did, in fact, get first hand information in the areas in which they travelled. In fact, what they have said constitutes a very good reflection of the views of

people living in those areas. The solutions that they propose appear to be, in most instances at least, logical and sensible, ones that the government ought to pursue. So I have no hesitation in saying that, certainly in principle, the ideas expressed make a good deal of sense.
I was also delighted to have the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador acknowledge that in the case of highways, and in the case of some of the other recommendations contained in the report, these are not matters that are completely within the competence of the federal government. There is in the case of the roads proposals, as in some others, the necessity to consult with the various provincial governments, and even with some of the municipalities. Indeed, there are other places where even private interests are involved. In one or two cases one might question whether or not the recommendations come within the purview of the federal government at all. I have in mind the last of the recommendations having to do with the current status of the Carol Lake Company Act, which it could conceivably be argued is a matter relating wholly and exclusively to the provincial government. I am not certain of that but that will be a point worth examining.
My main reason for making these comments is to point out that in all cases we will be more than prepared to make the studies that the report recommends. On balance, as Minister of Transport, I feel that many of the recommendations are sound. As the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador has said, in one or two cases we have already proceeded to implement these recommendations. Certainly, I see no reason why we should not look into the others.
Again, let me emphasize that in virtually all of the recommendations there is, in addition to the need to consult with, for example, provincial governments and other agencies, the necessity for feasibility studies to be made. There is also some question of jurisdiction in the matter, for instance, of the ferry from the north shore to the south shore of the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Again, this is one of those issues where it is not clear in my mind whether it is a federal responsibility or requires the initiation of the provincial government which will be helped through some form of subsidy program, if that turns out to be the logical answer to the problem. Similarly, in the case of other proposals, it will be necessary to discuss whether this method would provide the solution.

I have received, as I believe the committee have, representations suggesting that the real answer in terms of that part of the country is perhaps an extension of the roads system. Therefore, within the whole complex of these first class recommendations, I am sure that the committee members, as well as the members of the House, recognize the need for the studies they propose.
On the question of airline activities in northern Quebec and Labrador, here again there is some question as to the competence of any government agency to require that, for example, the two airlines pool their activities. This recommendation pretty well parallels one that was made by the Canadian Transport Commission itself at the time that these licences were granted. It will be necessary in this case to see whether or not we have the power or the authority in any agency of the federal government to force them to do this if they do not feel so inclined.
I want to express my very great regret that these airlines have not, in fact, as yet seen fit to carry out this suggestion of the Canadian Transport Commission. Quite frankly, I am disappointed that it has taken so long for them to do so. As yet I have not found any clear cut explanation on the part at least of one of the airlines concerned why that is so. I am told that one of the airlines is quite happy and is prepared to do so. However, I simply make this point of order to emphasize that it may not be something that we are in a position to require two carriers to do. If we can do so, then I will not be in the least hesitant to utilise my maximum authority, because what the committee has recommended does make an enormous amount of sense.
All of this is simply by way of saying that I and the government would have no compunction whatever about accepting the hon. member's motion. In giving concurrence to the committee report, I want to emphasize what I said before. Concurrence on the part of the government in this motion involves our acknowledgement of the valuable work that has been done by the committee in examining transportation conditions in eastern Canada. It involves the acknowledgement that the work was thorough and that many reasoned recommendations resulted. By concurring in the motion, the government also agrees that the committee's recommendations deserve, and will get, full consideration in terms of the implementation of policy. To the extent that our competence, budgetary conditions and general policies permit, as well as, of course, in terms of the limitations of our jurisdiction,

A specific mention is made in the report about ferryboats. The minister said earlier that he did not know whether ferryboats were under the federal or the provincial jurisdiction. I know that after many efforts to secure a ferryboat service between the south shore and the north shore we have always been told, at least these last few years, that those ferryboats provided a provincial service and that, consequently, jurisdiction over them ought to rest with the province of Quebec.
The ferryboats system also comes under the federal jurisdiction, I think. In fact, all ferryboats in Canada, whether they are provincial or interprovincial services, have always been subject to federal interventions and in some cases, the federal government has subsidized them. I can hardly understand why this government would not do the same in an area where industry is very active and where ferryboats services are very much needed.
Mention is also of the ports at Baie-Comeau and Sept-iles. I would like to say a few words about the latter. The committee members, including some opposition members, in particular the representative of the New Democratic party, came to visit the Sept-iles harbour and they all agreed that it did not meet the actual requirements of maritime traffic.
For the past three years, in keeping with the recommendations, I have been trying to get a new dock for this seaport from which 25 million tons of ore were shipped last year, giving it first place for shipping volume. An increase of some four million tons is expected this year, which means total shipments of some 30 million tons.


It is therefore most urgent that another dock be added to the present port facilities and I again ask that the Minister of Transport try to convince of this necessity the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) who over the past three years has been against the building of this new dock.
My colleagues from Newfoundland have commented on air transportation. I would add that some of the recommendations proposed extending the Baie-Comeau airport and I hope the minister will take good note of them.
When it comes to roads, I must say that everywhere the committee members travelled on this vast territory they expressed the desire that the isolated mining towns would be linked by a road network. I know that roads come under provincial jurisdiction, but if we examine the committee recommendations we see that they favor an agreement between the Newfoundland and Quebec governments in respect of road construction.
I think it is the responsibility of the federal as well as the provincial governments to get these very active and hard working populations out of their isolation. Once on the site, we talked a lot about roads. Of course, the committee then explained that the roads department came under the jurisdiction of the provincial government.
As far as the other transportation systems are concerned, the committee heard some evidence and received more than 60 briefs. The committee then replied to witnesses that television was the responsibility of the Department of Communications.
The inhabitants, who are increasing in number from year to year, in view of the gigantic developments, are still without a television network. I think the government should look seriously into this matter, which seems to have been the case for a few years, but they have not yet come up with any suggestion.
I am glad to note that the House accepts unanimously the recommendations of this report. In visiting my constituency the committee has done an excellent job. I am convinced that the people acknowledge that. They were pleased to see members of Parliament coming to them, as they are not usually want to do, in order to assess local problems.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF STANDARDS, APPOINTMENT OF INSPECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the privilege, on behalf of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro), of introducing in the House of Commons, for consideration by hon. members, Bill S-14, an act respecting the sale and importation of certain radiation emitting devices. This bill, which was introduced earlier this session in the Senate, was studied by the Senate Committee on Health, Science and Welfare and was given third reading and passed by the Senate on February 19, 1970.
In this age of rapid technological progress, we have witnessed, among other things, an electronic explosion. This technology, connected with electro-magnetic radiation and its many applications in the fields of medicine, industry, education and entertainment, has been accompanied by many dangers. The Department of National Health and Welfare has, for some years, been involved in the health aspect of the use of radioactive substances and recently has become increasingly aware of the need for control in the design and sale of devices which emit electro-magnetic radiation.
Bill S-14 deals specifically with the sale and importation of devices that may produce and emit dangerous radiation. It will enable the Governor in Council to establish minimum safety standards with respect to the design and construction of radiation devices not involving atomic energy or radioactivity, which are already controlled under the Atomic Energy Control Act. The purpose of the bill is to protect the public from a particularly insidious hazard; for example, exposure to radiation that may escape from the device and harm people in the vicinity.
Radiation is a broad term. The bill refers to electromagnetic and ultrasonic radiation. The radiation-emitting devices covered by this definition include x-ray machines, microwave ovens, laser generators and ultra-sound equipment. It also includes certain electronic devices which emit radiation as an unwanted by-product of their operation. None of these instruments, designed principally for scientific, medical and industrial use, are presently subject to federal control.
[Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) .1

The need for safety standards for radiation equipment has been recognized for many years. Radioactive devices are strictly controlled under the Atomic Energy Control Regulations. The other forms of radiation, equally dangerous, should be subject to similar safety restrictions. Many scientists in Canada and other countries have urged the necessity for this, and for good reason, because the effects of radiation on health are particularly serious.
It is well known, for example, that exposure to even small amounts of radiation can increase the incidence of leukemia and cancer and produce genetic damage. Although the experts in this field cannot give, in quantitative terms, a precise measure of the number of persons affected, they are convinced that even low level emissions, so-called "stray" or "leakage" radiation, adds in some degree to the statistical incidence of these diseases. The seriousness of these effects, even where the risk is low, makes it imperative to hold radiation emissions to the very lowest levels possible. To do so, standards must be set and maintained by regulatory control.
Particularly important is the provision of standards governing the design and construction of the devices. They apply before the device is put to use and constitute the basic first line of protection. It is with such standards that Bill S-14 is concerned. Proper design of equipment can often reduce unwanted exposures very significantly without impairing the usefulness of the device. Appropriate standards for this purpose have been recommended by scientists associated with the World Health Organization and other international agencies.
Not all these recommendations, even the very simplest, are being followed at the present time in Canada. In the case of x-rays, for example, a recent survey of dental x-ray units in the Ottawa area, carried out by the Department of National Health and Welfare, showed that a large percentage of the x-ray machines in use had one or more shortcomings, as judged by the recommended standard, which could result in unnecessary exposure to patient or to the operator.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
Microwaves, in addition to their use in radar and communication networks, are finding extensive application in commercial equipment such as ovens and dryers. They are used in automatic food vending machines, restaurant kitchens and many industrial operations where fast drying or heating is needed.
March 6. 1970
111 effects reported in humans include eye cataracts, blood changes and disturbance of the nervous system. Evidence of a statistical increase in the incidence of eye cataracts among persons exposed to microwave emissions has been documented.
To prevent such adverse health effects, international agencies have established recommended standards with respect to radiation emissions, that is, the leakage radiation. Nevertheless, in a recent survey carried out by the United States department of health, education and welfare, it was found that a substantial proportion of the microwave ovens tested emitted radiation in excess of the standard. The Department of National Health and Welfare is currently conducting a survey of ovens and dryers in the greater Ottawa area and has found some similar deficiencies.
Laser devices are now extensively used in hospitals and in industry. Furthermore, they are being sold to educational institutions as teaching aids. This type of device is relatively new and uses are being developed rapidly. The small, but very intense beam of laser light is known to be particularly harmful to the eyes. Clinical evidence of damage to the retina of the eye, caused by accidentally viewing inadequately safeguarded equipment, has been reported in the United States and in other countries.
Ultrasonic devices are finding many applications in medical practice and in industry. Until recently it was thought that the passage of ultrasonic energy through the body, as carried out in medical diagnostic procedures, is not hazardous, but recently there have been reports of experiments on animals which indicate an effect on growth patterns. There is also some indication that ultrasonic radiation can interact with reproductive cells in a way which could produce genetic defects.
The bill, therefore, covers a wide range of devices which are used primarily for industrial, medical and scientific applications. It will ensure that defective, sub-standard equipment is kept off the market. This, of course, is only one aspect of the radiation protection problem. Other aspects such as safe installation and operation are not dealt with in the bill because they come under provincial jurisdiction. Some provinces have already passed legislation along these fines. Bill S-14 can be considered as complementary to, not conflicting with, these provincial regulations.
Radiation Emitting Devices Bill
Finally, I should mention that the bill is drawn in a way which envisages the introduction of regulations on a gradual, step-bystep basis. Specific categories of devices will have to be defined and standards established for each. There will be ample opportunity for discussion with manufacturers as to any modifications necessary to meet the standard proposed. This procedure is possible because the hazard is viewed as, principally, a long term one. Adverse health effects would be expected only after very long periods of exposure. Therefore, except ini unusual cases, it is unlikely that the introduction of standards will necessitate immediate and drastic design changes in present models.
When Bill S-14, after receiving second reading in this House, is studied in detail by the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, I expect to introduce an amendment to subclause (h) of clause 2, changing the definition of radiation emitting device so that it will mean any device which emits radiation. In this way, devices such as television sets may be included in the regulations to the act if approved by the Governor in Council.
Bill S-14 is an important piece of legislation and one more step taken by this government, and particularly by the Department of National Health and Welfare, to protect the health of the Canadian people. On behalf of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, I commend this legislation to all hon. members, as it is in the public interest.

speechtext:
I trust the Minister of Agriculture will remain here during this discussion. I see him behind the curtain. As long as he stays, it will be all right; we do not want to lose him now for another 25 minutes.
The Parliamentary Secretary has given an explanation of this bill. It will, of course be referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs where it will receive a careful and more detailed examination. I have read the bill and I do not find much there with which to quarrel.
The Parliamentary Secretary told us that this measure would cover X-ray machines, microwave ovens and certain laser beam installations. I can understand that danger might be involved in handling these things- that dangerous radiations might be emitted, and that some provision is necessary. The Parliamentary Secretary mentioned that surveys were being conducted in the Ottawa area and that some deficiencies have been

4484	COMMONS
Radiation Emitting Devices Bill discovered. I agree that action should be taken to protect the public in this respect. I am pleased to note that, generally speaking, equipment presently in use will not be affected by the legislation. The Parliamentary Secretary intimated, to the best of his ability I gather, that most of the equipment presently in use would not have to be discarded. So, no monetary penalty win be incurred by present users.
I am wondering just where television sets might fit into this legislation. Wiould they come under the Hazardous Products Act, or would they be dealt with here? I was pleased to hear the hon. gentleman mention that the regulations would be brought in step by step, on a gradual basis. I note clause 12(2) suggests that reasonable opportunity will be afforded to manufacturers, distributors and other interested persons to make representations to the minister. We are in favour of this.
There is one clause, however, with which I have to disagree. I refer to clause 13, which simply means that an accused is guilty until he has proved his innocence. This seems to reflect a trend of thinking which has been developing in government circles. To my mind, this is not justice. I believe it is up to the Crown to prove guilt. The clause reads:
In any prosecution for an offence under this Act, it is sufficient proof of the offence to establish that it was committed by an employee or agent of the accused whether or not the employee or agent is identified or has been prosecuted for the offence, unless the accused establishes that the offence was committed without his knowledge or consent and that he exercised all due diligence to prevent its commission.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
This puts the onus directly on the accused to prove that he did not know his employee or agent might have been guilty of some offence. I think it is for the Crown to prove that the accused must have known. As far as I can see, the trend today in government activities is that the authorities seem to feel they, themselves, are above the law. The income tax department have been carrying on this way for years, and I just do not like it. We are putting the finger of guilt on the accused until he proves that he is innocent, something that I think is a very unfortunate, indeed a bad, trend.
With those few remarks I will resume my seat; when the bill does reach committee, closer examination of its details will be made.

Recently in the House it was announced that assistance would be given to the western wheat producers not to grow wheat. I take no exception to that at all, though I doubt very much whether the proposals that were announced will do the job the government intends them to do. Be that as it may, a certain amount of money is going to be spent in assisting western wheat producers.
The Wheat Producers Marketing Board of Ontario feel that the wheat producers of Ontario should not be left out of the picture altogether. In view of the government's failure to sell western grain, it is becoming quite obvious that many western farmers are going to diversify and go into some other type of farming operation, mainly the feeding of livestock. This will no doubt create a hardship for the eastern farmers by diminishing the traditional role that they have considered to be theirs.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
This was part of the reason Eastern farmers requested this amendment to allow the minister to guarantee loans to the Wheat Producers Marketing Board of Ontario, who will make initial payments to farmers. This guarantee of initial payments will be, in effect, a floor price. The Wheat Producers Marketing Board of Ontario has done a tremendous job of moving the wheat that has been grown by the producers. Oftentimes, in fact most of the time, all this wheat has to be kept in storage for considerable lengths of time until markets can be found. When mar-
Agricultural Co-operative Marketing Act kets are found, it is helpful if there is a considerable amount of wheat in storage to fill these orders. This is the traditional method of marketing that has developed in the last three years.
A charge of 17 cents a bushel is deducted to pay the storage costs. This amount has been sufficient to cover the cost up to now, but beginning in the next crop year 17 cents a bushel will not be sufficient to pay the storage costs and also fulfil the subsidized contracts for export sales that are necessary to move the wheat. Because of this fact a request has been made by the Ontario Wheat Producers that Ontario grain, particularly wheat, come under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act in order that government funds could be used to pay part of the storage costs that are entailed in the marketing of this wheat.
I should like to ask the minister if it would be possible, under this legislation, for the government to pay a certain portion of the storage costs that are necessary in the marketing of wheat from Ontario. Really, we are asking for no more than the western wheat producer receives. I believe the government pays the storage charges on everything over 178 million bushels, which would mean at the present time it is paying the storage charges on close to one billion bushels. I do not think this is too much for the Ontario farmer to ask. I should like to ask the minister, either now or at some later time, to give us an indication of the possibility of something like this being done to assist the eastern producer.

the provinces of Ontario and Quebec on the terms under which a National Capital Region Transit Authority could be created and incorporated by federal charter bearing in mind (a) the inadequacy of public transportation facilities in the national capital region (b) the restriction by charter of transit services, both publicly and privately owned, to municipal boundaries (c) the need for longterm planning of an integrated system of rail rapid transit, bus and other means of urban transit (d) the crises developed by the unfair competition provided by public subsidies on behalf of private vehicles (e) the contribution by an efficient, low-cost public transportation system to the balanced economic and social development of the whole national capital region.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion is put forward for consideration and public debate at this time. I hope hon. members will judge it in relation to two bills which stand in my name on the Order Paper-Bill C-57, to establish a National Capital Region Planning Board and Bill C-112, to establish a National Capital Region Pollution Control Board. These two measures, together with the present one which would create a regional transit authority, are based on certain assumptions. The first is that following a recommendation of the Federal-Provincial Conference of February, 1969, the form of article 16 of the British North America Act will be altered to provide for the inclusion of an area in the province of Quebec and a'n area in the province of Ontario which will correspond roughly to the area defined in the act establishing the national capital region. In other words, the unanimous agreement which was exhibited at the conference where the report dealing with this matter was tabled persuades me that we should consider, when planning the future form of the capital, an area of roughly that size.
The second assumption is that a federal district such as Washington or Brasilia will not be created. In its place will be a development of two municipalities, the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton, which has been created on the Ontario side by act of the provincial legislature of Ontario and which is now well under way with a good start, and on the Quebec side the communaute Outaouaise which has been created by act of the provincial legislature of Quebec and which is now in process of development.
These two municipalities, I confidently predict, will develop according to the cultural and legal patterns which reflect the duality of Canadian life. On the Ontario side, I fully expect that the civil law as it affects property and other matters will continue to be that which prevails in the province of Ontario,

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take the opportunity of saying a few words about the speech of the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis). I agree in most part with what the hon. member has put to the House. He mentioned the problem of pollution. It is my understanding that the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec are not acting in the manner they should to correct the problem of pollution of the Ottawa River. I hope in the near future these two governments will reconsider their position and get together with the federal government to find a solution.
I am not clear about one point in relation to what the hon. member for Ottawa West said. He talked about a transit system for the city of Ottawa. Two or three weeks ago it was announced in the House that a new bridge would be built across the Ottawa River. I know the hon. member was a member of the Ottawa city council for a number of years and may be more aware of the situation than
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Bechard).]
I am, but I am wondering whether this bridge is being taken into consideration in the plans for the type of transit system we would like to have in Ottawa.
Urban transit has become a serious problem in metropolitan areas of Canada. Everyone who has ever had the ulcer-inducing experience of rush hour traffic in Toronto, Ottawa, Hamilton, Montreal, Quebec or Vancouver is all too familiar with the problem. Statistics are available to outline the congestion. One-half of all Canadians presently live in metropolitan areas with populations of over 100,000, and by 1980 it is estimated that one-third of all Canadians will live in Montreal, Toronto or Vancouver. Passenger motor vehicle registration has soared by over 70 per cent in the last ten years. In the past our main response to this growing congestion has been the construction and extension of massive freeway systems.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
However, there are definite disadvantages to these systems. The costs are astronomical. Valuable land is consumed by costly expropriation and is thereby removed from municipal tax rolls. Parking space becomes a major problem, especially in the business core. Actual construction costs skyrocket. The elevated portion of the Gardiner Expressway in Toronto cost $16 million per mile. Most urban planners now agree that as an efficient means of carrying people within metropolitan areas, the automobile finishes dead last and that reliance on it should be reduced in favour of rapid public transit systems.
Chicago's Congress Street Expressway provides a good example of cost comparisons between freeway and rapid transit systems. This system consists of an eight-lane expressway and a two-track transit line. The tracks occupy one-fifth of the right-of-way and have a capacity of 30,000 seated passengers per hour, while the expressway occupies four-fifths of the right-of-way and accommodates a maximum capacity of 9,000 people per hour. The expressway cost $188.5 million, in comparison with $36 million for the transit line.
In Toronto there is the subway which was constructed not too many years ago. I think it serves very well the city of Toronto. There also are the go-go trains which were recently installed there. When the hon. member for Ottawa West spoke in introducing the bill, I wondered whether he had in mind these rapid transit systems or expressways for the city of Ottawa. As I have shown, there is quite
March 6. 1970

a spread in the cost between the two. I certainly think that when the various governments get together on this matter they should look very carefully into the cost and consider which system would be most beneficial to the area.
Montreal has a fairly new subway. There are also suburban trains which bring passengers in from Rigaud, Vaudreuil, Ste. Anne and other places along the line. Thousands of passengers are carried on those trains. The hon. member for Ottawa West said it is a good idea to have a system such as I have in mind when I speak of expressways and rapid transit lines. I think this system has been of great benefit to the city of Montreal, where you can see thousands of people leaving the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific stations to go to their offices.
I hope that when the regional, provincial and federal governments get together to consider a transit system for Ottawa they will study the matter in great detail in order to come up with the best answer. I certainly agree with my hon. friend that there should be a better transit system in the city of Ottawa.

National Capital Region Transit Authority
In fact, I cannot understand how it is that we are not any better off as regards transportation in the national capital than we were a hundred years ago.
Mr. Speaker, when talking about the national capital, one generally remembers the Greber plan which was tabled in the House in 1951 and was the beginning of a planned development to make of the national capital a model for the whole country.
Several recommendations of the Greber plan have been implemented, but many others have not. For instance, as regards transportation in the Hull area, railroad tracks have been removed. Trains no longer cross the city, except perhaps the one known as "the northern train" which stops at the Hull station. Thus the city of Hull has a station where very few trains stop.
We can now do something in the field of transportation because there are two regional governments, one in Ontario and the other in Quebec. In my opinion, obstacles to agreement have been removed, since the 22 municipalities of Western Quebec are now represented by a regional government, just as are the five municipalities on the Ontario side. Nothing therefore prevents the establishment of a committee to study the problem of public transit in the area of the national capital. The federal government should create it or support it. The national capital should set an example, but, our transportation system is unfortunately a real disaster, because transportation today is a technical problem. When money has to be spent, it should be spent wisely. There has never been any long term planning on the problem of transportation in the national capital region, because the three levels of government never reached an agreement.
It is easy to build bridges but I think that bridges should only serve to unite two road systems; otherwise they become useless. If we build a bridge without paying much attention to the problem of approaches, we may create traffic-jam problems.
The best example of such a lack of logic in 1970 was that we had a highway plan for Hull, which was not accepted on account of disagreements between municipalities. In the end, we had to face a situation where two bridges were built parallel to one another, as is the case in Gatineau Point. So we have traffic jams on both sides.
Can we call that long-term planning? Not at all. If we want to indulge in long-term

National Capital Region Transit Authority planning, we must build bridges of course, as the need arises, like around the Island of Hull. Moreover, the Britannia suburbs must be linked to the municipality of Deschenes so as to relieve the traffic congestion. Along the Aylmer Road, even a casual glance will show that we are 100 years behind the times in our area. However, we are part of the national capital area.
When I spoke about long-term planning, I said that no announcement should ever be made regarding the construction of bridges or roads without being sure that the project can be incorporated to a broad highway system.
My hon. friend from Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) mentioned another problem. Longterm planning is a good thing and I hope that we shall go into it. However, short-term planning is also required. By 1972, many Ottawa residents will go to work in the Hull area, but if some rapid means of transportation are not available, connected with the systems in operation on both sides of the river, we shall face in our national capital the greatest traffic tie up ever seen before in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I have proposed a monorail. Of course, there are other means of transportation, but my suggestion is based on technological data. Within the framework of the Canadian Transport Commission, has been established an agency called the Research and Development Unit on Urban Transportation within the Transport Department.
This body is set up in view of developing national methods of approaching the problem of transport in the towns of Canada and eventually solving them.
Canada cannot maintain a sound economy if traffic tie-ups and ill-adjusted public transportation jeopardize the productivity of our towns. Considering that urban transportation absorbs about a fifth of the cost of the whole urban economy, the measures intended to improve their efficiency can not only benefit the national economy but also improve the standards of living of most Canadians.
The Canadian Transport Commission set up this body in 1968. I wonder what part the Transport Commission was able to play in this respect, now that urban transportation is


based on technology. Indeed there are now new means of transport, made available to the public such as the hovercraft, or vacuum tubes where fast trains would be able to be run in air-tight tunnels; there are helicopters and also STOL planes.
A lot of studies have also been conducted on the monorail and the underground. The problem is therefore to use in the best possible way the existing means of transportation, even if this means considering the implementation of traffic rules and the development of a utilitarian urbanization, which in the present trend have already resulted in a comprehensive program.
Just think of those who apply modern technology. I am thinking of the French lineal "Urba-IV" motor, based on the suction principle a type of "hovercraft" in reverse that does extraordinary things. It is the motor of the future seeing it weighs next to nothing.
Since modern technology has been applied, wonderful results have been achieved. The London-Manchester Railway line was electrified, in England; this resulted for British Railways in a 54 per cent increase in the traffic, and 40 per cent in income in the first year of operations, of the new express trains, in 1966.
The great speed of the "Capital", the famous train between Paris and Tolouse, was the direct cause of a 42 per cent increase in the traffic on that line. In Japan, the inauguration of the train "Toka'ido" fooled all the experts by reducing the air traffic between Tokyo and Nagoya to such an extent that the service had to be interrupted.
Just recently, I was reading in Aviation Week and Space Technology that American Airlines was considering the possibility of abandoning its New York-Washington line because, as a result of the competition of express trains such as the "Metroline", it is no longer profitable.
The situation is much the same wherever modern technology has been applied. What is the research division of the Transport Commission looking for? I do not know. Perhaps some day it will bring forth something that has been gestating quietly in the dark. However, it is responsible for not applying modern technology to a rapid transit system between Ottawa and Hull. This is the national capital, yet no one has thought of that. I feel so strongly about this, that I think the chairman of the Transport Commission should resign.
March 6, 1970

When the first national transport conference was held at the Royal York in Toronto, someone said this, and I quote:

The government of Canada Is convinced that urban transportation is essentially a responsibility of provincial governments.

This may be true in theory, but not in practice, because it is up to the central government to update transport technology today, since it has set up a research division within the Canadian Transport Commission.
On the other hand, and this is where I see the prostitution-

Canadian Transport Commission president J. W. Pickersgill presented the semi-official Ottawa attitude in the usual terms:	stressing that urban
transportation was essentially a provincial matter and the federal government, constitutionally, could not interfere. He carefully avoided any commitment to provide federal funds for developing subways and other means of mass transit.
And just to be on the safe side-though he denied this later-Pickersgill cut from his prepared speech the one paragraph the 1,000 delegates wanted to hear.
What he did not say was this: "Since adequate, efficient and economical urban transportation is just as necessary to the national well-being as adequate, efficient and economical extra-urban and international transport, it is the proper concern of the government of Canada".

Since the Canadian Transport Commission has voted funds for the research section, what are we waiting for to do something? Concurrently with the Greber report, transportation studies have been made and should have been published in 1966. Nothing has been done, even if several thousand dollars were spent.
Recently, the Quebec government has decided to undertake a transportation study in Hull. When are we going to write our exams, Mr. Speaker? When will we finally understand that we are not living for structures, but to help our fellow-men?
When bridges are built, the use of cars is encouraged, the air becomes more polluted and people get on each other's nerves even more. Psychiatric problems are created. People are frustrated at having to wait several hours on bridges when traffic is heavy.
I proposed building a monorail. This is a modern and futuristic solution to the problem, and I am not alone to suggest it. Mr. 4501
National Capital Region Transit Authority Fullerton, the present chairman of the National Capital Commission, formerly financial analyst for the newspaper La Presse, in an article dated February 17, 1969, and entitled: "Cities should promote public transit", said the following:
Evidently, it is costly to build new rail systems. However, a monorail system for suspension-trains would permit significant savings on the cost of ground space. The hon. member for Hull, Mr. Gaston Isabelle, incidentally, has just recommended that type of transportation to provide a more convenient link between Ottawa and Hull. It really seems that the monorail is in a fair way to asserting itself as the ultimate solution to the problems of transportation between cities and suburbs.
That man now holds the office of Chairman of the National Capital Commission: we will see what he can do in this area.
In Canada, it is claimed that it is not for the government to consider those things and to allocate funds to further technology so that the transportation means at our disposal are as adequate as those existing in Europe. In this respect, the November 1966 issue of International Science and Technology published an article entitled New Transportation Technology. It says the following, and I quote:
c (4:40 p.m.)

No really new technology is ready to go yet. But a lot of technology will get further development now that the federal funds are becoming available.

That was the situation in the United States in 1966. I suggest we should follow the example of that country with regard to transportation. Intensive research is carried out there. For this, the Americans deserve congratulations.
Today, there must be agreement. Yes, as there are two regional governments, we should, with the help of the National Capital Commission, carry out a study on the creation of a public transportation system, in order to put a stop to the present situation where the people are penalized because governements have not carried out their responsibilities.
I alluded a moment ago to the establishment of two regional administrations. Does the public know when this project was first considered? It was in 1946 and recommendations to that effect were submitted in 1947. The Ottawa Planning Board also promoted this idea in Toronto. This concept was accepted two years ago, Mr. Speaker.
In the province of Quebec, they have just approved the creation of a regional government. It took almost 25 years to finalize such

Before concluding my remarks, I wish to point out that in France, at the present time, they are putting the finishing touch on the famous Bertin aero tram that is to run at a speed of 350 kilometres per hour and will be used between Paris and Orleans. If the Canadian Transport Commission goes on beating about the bush, I shall recommend to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) to make an airbus available to me so that I might go over there and see with my own eyes what is going on. I do not know if they are aware of it, but I was told they were looking into the same problems as we are. For years now the linear engine URBA-IV has been under consideration in Paris and Lyon. Here studies are starting all over again.
The Canadian Transport Commission, instead of suggesting the construction of a subway, ignores the matter completely, as evidenced at the first national conference on transportation, held at the Royal York Hotel just as if we were still in 1929. I think that our organizations lack responsible leaders. It is said that often parliament moves slowly due to its age-long tradition, perhaps, and its obsolete customs. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to congratulate my friend, the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) who speaks, as everybody knows, with special authority on this matter. This derives from his long experience in municipal affairs in Ottawa, and also from his special knowledge as a former member of the Ottawa Transport Commission.
I also wish to speak in support of this motion, as have my friends, the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Code), the hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather) and the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle). In addressing myself to this problem, hon. members will understand it is not just a local problem, it is a national problem, and that we are confronted in this country finally and fortunately with an important change in public attitude.
For many, many years public transit has been regarded as a second best. But now people are beginning to see that public transit is a necessity; and more than that, it is a more desirable alternative than the proliferation of travel by motor car. What people are finally seeing is what the hon. member for Ottawa West referred to as the hidden cost of motor car travel. This has always been hidden, and it has to be balanced against the exposed cost of public transit, which is out in the open. Public transit has suffered; the people have suffered. But I hope we have at last come to the time when the people generally share the views expressed here, that rational choices have to be made in order to re-organize the total transportation system, not only of this area but of every metropolitan area in Canada.
The costs, which are now apparent, of the proliferation of motor car travel include clogged highways, congestion, the turning of our downtown areas virtually into parking lots, pollution, accidents and the ever-increas-in expense necessary to meet the requirements of private motor car travel. One authority who participated in the conference to which the hon. member for Hull referred,
March 6, 1970

the first Canadian Urban Transportation Conference, Dr. Joseph Kates, referred to this problem as follows:
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
We have private car oriented developments and we are becoming increasingly dependent on the private car. This marvellous flexible machine, the dream of everyone who hasn't one, the luxury conveyance with its image of freedom, flexibility and status is also becoming the Frankenstein monster who frequently dominates our life and our cities and forces us to pay a very, very high price for its convenience. What is this price we pay?
I do not wish to expand on that price, but people are becoming aware of what it is. The controversy over the Spadina development in Toronto, which is matched in Ottawa by the controversy over a proposal to run a freeway through the centre of the city, indicates to all sections of our population the price we pay in trying to accommodate the ever-increasing number of private cars. We see this in many ways.
I quote further the words of Dr. Kates, who speaks about the situation in metropolitan Toronto and whose remarks on the total cost of all private car travel might be of interest to the House:
The utilization of our huge investment in private cars is unbelievably low. The car fleet in metropolitan Toronto alone represents an investment of several billions of dollars, the garages, carports and parking lots required to store these cars represent a further investment of several billions of dollars, the roads, bridges and tunnels required for these cars represent a further several billions of dollars and the costs of operating, maintaining and repairing this huge fleet amount to perhaps another $500 million annually.
Yet this huge investment is used on the average perhaps one to two hours a day, or less than 10 per cent, representing an enormous wasteful use of expensive resources which could be used in so many other ways to make us stronger and richer. When this low utilization of the car is multiplied by the low utilization of its seats we find that the huge investment has a utilization of less than 2 per cent.
While as individuals we are frequently willing to buy expensive cars, often a little beyond our means, as a society we find ourselves financially in serious trouble in meeting the requirements of these cars in terms of roads, bridges and tunnels, and parking facilities.
Mr. Speaker, I am not suggesting that we can legislate the private car out of existence. This is clearly impossible in a free society. As the hon. member for Ottawa West pointed out, the obvious solution is to provide a transit system wherein people will have an opportunity to express a reasonable preference between public transit and the use of their private automobiles. There is experience to 21774-8J
DEBATES	4503
National Capital Region Transit Authority show that where these reasonable alternatives are provided, people will prefer public transit. For example, it is estimated that 85 per cent of the commuter traffic within range of the new GO transit system outside Toronto use that transit system.
Despite the difficulties of our local transit commission in Ottawa it has been shown that by improving the services and providing better facilities, greater utilization occurs. In another paper presented to this conference, Dr. Kates had this to say:
In Canada, transit organizations have also made important progress. The Ottawa Transit Commission, for example, has introduced new bus shelters, extended routes, provided more frequent service and introduced better vehicles. The result is a significant increase in the number of passengers.
The hon. member for Ottawa West referred to the fact that this significant increase occurred over a period of four or five years. Mr. Speaker, the problem we face in this area is clearly one of attacking transit on an areawide basis; it cannot be attacked on the basis of solving it within local municipal boundaries. It is not an easy problem to solve; it requires study, co-operation and experimentation. Nor can it be solved by trying to impose arbitrary penalties on one section of the population as opposed to another. It will not be solved for example, by imposing penalties on public servants in respect of their parking privileges when there are no public transit facilities from the suburbs to bring people to work. The basic problem in my constituency on the outskirts of Ottawa, which includes Nepean township, is that there are no public transit facilities. The Ottawa Transit Commission comes to the fringe of the area at Bay-shore and Parkwood Hills but the rest of this important suburban development, which has upwards of 40,000 people, is not served by any public transit at all.
